newsitem.title: DENMARK: Nordic ministers plan joint strategy on biker war.
newsitem.headline: Nordic ministers plan joint strategy on biker war.

text.p: Justice Ministers from Finland, Norway, Sweden and Denmark meet in Copenhagen on Friday to seek a joint strategy against a motorcycle gang war that has brought blood and destruction to all four countries.
No agenda for the talks had been finalised by Thursday but justice ministry officials expected the meeting to produce firm plans for action.

The visitors will also seek full details of a Danish law passed on Thursday designed to drive biker clubhouses out of urban areas, where other residents fear being caught in the crossfire in battles between their unwanted neighbours.
Finland's minister Laila Freivalds, Norway's Grete Faremo, Finland's Kari Hakamies and Denmark's Bjoern Westh will consider if the same or similar laws should be introduced in their countries.

They may also come up with fresh thinking on how to combat the gangs, which have flourished in the Nordic countries in part because of the region's flabby gun laws, high respect for due legal process and tolerance of unconventional behaviour.
Senior Nordic police officers already regularly discuss the spiralling violence in the turf war between the dominant Hell's Angels gang and the rival Bandidos.

Police advise one another of cross-border movements of gang members, although sometimes too late. Danish and Norwegian Bandidos returning from a visit to Finland were ambushed by a rival gang outside Copenhagen and Oslo aiports before Finnish police could flash a warning of their impending arrival.
A Norwegian was wounded and Danish Bandido leader Uffe Hansen died in a hail of bullets.
Six suspects -- all Hell's Angels or with present or past links to the gang -- are in custody for the Copenhagen killing and due to go on trial in November.
Norway, Sweden and Finland share land frontiers and Denmark and Sweden are a 45-minute ferry ride apart.
Westh hastily called Friday's brainstorming session after a Sunday morning missile attack on the Hell's Angels' Copenhagen headquarters in which two people were killed.
One was a candidate for Hell's Angels membership, police said, the other a young mother with no known links to the gang attending an open-house party at their clubhouse, apparently out of curiosity.
Police regard the Bandidos, who have been battling the dominant Hell's Angels for close to three years, as the main suspect in Sunday's rocket attack.

The shoulder-fired anti-tank rocket used in the attack, and another abandoned unfired, were stolen from army stores in neighbouring Sweden in 1994. Other missiles from the break-in were fired at two Hell's Angels' clubhouses in different areas of Denmark last April.
Conflict between Hells' Angels and the Bandidos, both local offshoots of U.S. groups, arose almost as soon as the Bandidos set up shop in the region in the summer of 1993.

In February 1994 a member of the Hell's Angels-affiliated Rednecks died in a gunfight after walking -- reportedly by accident -- into a Bandidos meeting at a nightclub in the Swedish port of Helsingborg.

The then newly-elected president of the Bandidos, Mikael Ljunggren, was killed by a sniper as he rode his motorcycle north of the city in July 1995, in an ambush that investigators said could have been either a Hell's Angels attack or the work of fellow gang members opposed to his leadership.
In March this year, attackers shot dead a Bandidos leader in the Finnish capital, Helsinki, and the Copenhagen airport murder followed 10 days later.
A Danish Bandidos member was fatally shot in the head near the Norwegian town of Drammen in July.
